A blinded language-model screen for repeats in human proteins

McWhite Lab, Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of Arizona

We asked a language model, Gemini Carbon, to find repeats in human proteins by reading the sequences alone, i.e. using no code, no tools, no search and no protein names. While recognizing these patterns is extremely difficult for the human eye, we consider this to be a task that naturally suits the abilities of LLMs to recognize patterns in sequences. Repeats are especially common in disordered regions (Tompa, 2003; Simon & Hancock, 2009; Jorda et al., 2010). Many of the repeats in disordered or mixed sequence are short linear motifs (SLiMs), the short peptide modules that mediate many protein interactions in disordered regions (Van Roey et al., 2014).

Gallery of structured repeat architectures →
Disordered/mixed
Tandem arrayPRNP octarepeats: five PHGGGWGQ copies head to tail in the disordered N-terminal region. Their histidines bind copper ions.
Dispersed arrayNUP98 GLFG repeats: eight copies spread through the disordered FG region. They bind nuclear transport receptors and together form the selective barrier of the nuclear pore.

Why look for repeats in disordered regions?

Repeats can add function to proteins outside of structured regions:

  • Short linear motifs: many arrays are repeated copies of well-characterized SLiMs, peptide motifs of about 3–10 residues that bind partner proteins or mark sites for modification, such as the EH-domain-binding NPF motifs of EPN1 (Van Roey et al., 2014).
  • Multivalency: repeated binding motifs engage several partners at once, as the phosphotyrosines of LAT do in recruiting signaling proteins into condensates (Li et al., 2012; Su et al., 2016).
  • Collective properties: an array can act as a whole, as the FG repeats of NUP98 do in forming the selective barrier of the nuclear pore (Frey et al., 2006).
  • Longer units: repeat units can be much longer than canonical SLiMs, such as the 21-residue repeats of PRB4 (Kim et al., 1993).
  • Multisite modification: arrays provide many modification sites, as in the POLR2A CTD heptads that carry the CTD code (Buratowski, 2003) and the KSP repeats of NEFH.

Analysis of known and novel SLiMs

Known

?A repeat array is Known when the repeat itself is annotated in UniProt, curated in ELM, or described in a paper we can cite. Examples: the RNA polymerase II CTD heptads, neurofilament KSP repeats, nucleoporin GLFG units, prohormone cleavage repeats and curated docking motifs.

Known motif, new place

?The unit matches a specific motif class at the same position in at least 80% of copies. Most are docking motifs (SH2-binding tyrosines, NPF, IQ); the rest are modification sites at the same position in most copies.

In a functional region

Most copies sit inside a region that UniProt assigns a function to.?At least half of the copies lie inside a UniProt Region feature that names a function, such as an interaction with a partner protein, and no UniProt Repeat, Domain or Zinc finger feature covers them.

Novel

?No UniProt repeat, domain or region annotation, no curated ELM instance and no specific motif class. All are in disordered or mixed sequence.

Types of structured repeat

Most repeat arrays are folded domains in series (Marcotte et al., 1999). One example of each of the most common types.?UniProt already annotates these, so all are in the Known group. Their copy number is constrained by structure: a WD40 propeller closes with seven blades and EF-hands work in pairs. Types are ranked by how many repeat arrays they have, counting only types whose longest array has three or more copies. The example is the longest array of each type not already used for another tile; the bar shows its copies along the protein. Olduvai copies are coloured by subtype (copies grouped by sequence similarity).

Method

Gemini Carbon reads the sequences itself, with no tools, code, search or prior knowledge of named proteins. Scripts only select the cohort, blind the sequences and look up coordinates. A repeat array is the set of copies of one repeat in one protein.

1

Cohort

The full human proteome.

2

Blinding

Names and annotations are removed and sequences get shuffled anonymous IDs. The key is kept separately.

3

Reading

Four sequences per prompt: one pass for long structural repeats, then one over disordered stretches for short motifs.?Units of at least 5 aa in at least 3 copies; 2 copies only for long, conserved units.

4

Locating copies

The model quotes each copy exactly. A script finds each quote in the sequence; quotes that are not found are dropped.

5

Unblinding

Identities are attached only afterwards, then results are compared with UniProt features, ELM and AlphaFold models.

The prompt

System instructions

You are a protein sequence motif and repeat analyst examining blinded amino acid sequence(s).
STRICT ISOLATION RULE:
- Do NOT call any tools (do not read files, search the codebase, or search the web). Analyze ONLY the raw amino acid sequence text provided directly in the prompt.

Analysis guidelines:
- Use ZERO prior knowledge of specific proteins or named domain families; judge strictly from the amino acid sequence provided.
- Perform an explicit TWO-STAGE VISUAL SCAN on every sequence so strong structural repeats never shadow subtle disordered repeats:
  1. Stage 1 (Long & Structural Repeats): Scan the full sequence for longer repeats (15+ aa), tandem arrays, or high-conservation internal duplications.
  2. Stage 2 (Independent Disordered-Region Scan): Independently isolate all disordered-like regions (N/C-terminal tails, long linkers, segments enriched in P,S,E,K,Q,G,D,N,R,T and depleted in bulky hydrophobics) and carefully scan them for short-to-medium repeats (5-15 aa) occurring >=3 times, whether dispersed or tandem!
- Copy number & minimum length rule:
  - Minimum repeat unit length is strictly >=5 aa (never report <=4 aa short repeats).
  - Require >=3 occurrences by default (especially important for 5-15 aa repeats in disordered regions).
  - Report a 2-copy repeat ONLY if it is long (typically >=15 aa) and strongly conserved across many positions so chance occurrence is implausible.
- Spacing: Repeats do NOT need to be tandem or periodic -- dispersed repeats separated by variable linkers are equally important. Record whether spacing is "tandem" (head-to-tail or <=2 aa gap), "periodic" (regular linker length), or "dispersed" (variable spacing).
- Motif quality & low-complexity boundary:
  - Look for convincing multi-position architecture: fixed anchor residues (especially P, G, W, Y, F, C, H, D, E, K, R, L), constrained 2-3 residue choices, and physicochemically conserved positions.
  - Disregard pure unanchored low-complexity / compositional-bias tracts (bare homopolymers like QQQQQQ, PPPPPP, EEEEE, or simple 2-3 letter repeats like GSGSGS, RGG, SRSR with no multi-position consensus).
  - IMPORTANT EXCEPTION: Do NOT dismiss a motif merely because it contains a short proline or polar run (such as PPP or PPPP) IF it is anchored by conserved flanking or internal non-bias positions across >=3 copies (for example, `PPPPGφx[PG]L` or `[ST]Px+xΩ` where specific flanking residues align cleanly by eye).
- Window refinement & non-overlap:
  - Check whether shifting phase or expanding 1-4 residues left/right yields a longer, higher-information consensus across copies.
  - If a protein contains multiple distinct, non-overlapping repeat families (e.g., a structured repeat domain AND a dispersed 6-10mer motif in flanking disorder, or two different IDR motifs), report ALL of them, ordered strongest first. Never report overlapping instances.
- Proactive structural-bias `flags`:
  - Conventional tools easily detect collagen, coiled-coils, and charged helical rods. Whenever a sequence contains a noticeable tract of:
    * `"collagen_gxy"` (repetitive G-x-y triplets),
    * `"coiled_coil_heptad"` (amphipathic alpha-helical heptads with hydrophobic `a,d` register and polar/charged `e,g`), or
    * `"charged_helical_rod"` (extended E/K/R-rich single alpha-helical / charged alternating tracts like EEEKKRREEE...),
    add the corresponding label(s) to `flags`. Do NOT list those generic tracts in `repeats`, and continue scanning the rest of the protein for genuine motif/domain repeats.

Symbol key for `consensus` (1 token = 1 residue position, concatenated with NO separator):
  A..Y  = fixed standard amino acid (note: P is NOT part of φ; treat P as its own fixed anchor or inside [...])
  [XY]  = constrained choice of 2-3 specific amino acids (e.g., [ST], [GP], [KRH])
  φ     = hydrophobic, excluding proline (A,V,I,L,M,F,W,Y)
  ψ     = large aliphatic (V,I,L,M)
  Ω     = aromatic (F,W,Y)
  +     = basic / positively charged (K,R)
  -     = acidic / negatively charged (D,E)
  o     = polar uncharged (S,T,N,Q)
  x     = unconstrained single residue
  (For repeats >=20 aa with minor internal length variation across copies, use `(x){n,m}` only where a variable loop occurs.)

--- OUTPUT SCHEMA (per sequence) ---
{
  "seq_id": "<string: blinded sequence ID provided>",
  "has_repeat": <boolean: true if `repeats` is non-empty, else false>,
  "flags": ["collagen_gxy" | "coiled_coil_heptad" | "charged_helical_rod"],
  "repeats": [
    {
      "consensus": "<string using symbol key above>",
      "unit_length": <integer or "<min>-<max>" if variable-length >=20 aa repeat>,
      "spacing": "tandem" | "periodic" | "dispersed",
      "sequence_context": "disordered_like" | "structured_like" | "mixed",
      "confidence": "high" | "medium",
      "instances": [
        "<exact verbatim uppercase amino acid substring from the input sequence, in N-to-C order>"
      ],
      "rationale": "<concise 1-2 sentence explanation of conserved anchors, physicochemical positions, and spacing/context>"
    }
  ]
}

CRITICAL RULES:
1. Every string in `instances` MUST be an exact, contiguous, un-gapped substring copied verbatim from the input sequence.
2. Output ONLY valid JSON (a single object if 1 sequence is given, or a JSON array of objects if multiple sequences are given) -- no markdown fences, no prose.

Each request (four sequences)

Inspect these 4 anonymized human UniProt protein sequences strictly following your system instructions and output a JSON array of 4 objects (one per sequence, in order):

>SEQ_XXXXX length=342
M... (60-aa wrapped uppercase sequence)

>SEQ_YYYYY length=418
M...

Consensus notation. One symbol per residue position; unit positions in the highlights count these symbols from 1.

W fixed residue[ST] one of thesex any residue(x){4,13} variable loop φ hydrophobic (AVILMFWY)ψ large aliphatic (VILM)Ω aromatic (FWY) + basic (KR)- acidic (DE)o polar (STNQ)
